newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Jews blast Swiss on Holocaust fund appointments.
newsitem.headline: Jews blast Swiss on Holocaust fund appointments.

text.p: The World Jewish Congress (WJC) accused the Swiss government on Wednesday of not taking Jewish groups seriously by failing to confirm Nobel Peace Prize winner Elie Wiesel and two other nominees to head a Holocaust memorial find.

WJC chief negotiator Maram Stern said he was upset that a Swiss cabinet meeting on Wednesday had for the second week in a row skipped appointing the Jewish nominees for the fund's seven-member executive.
"Now they are playing with us. This is not serious," Stern, the WJC's assistant secretary-general, told Reuters by telephone from the organisation's European headquarters in Brussels.

WJC executive director Elan Steinberg said he was puzzled at why the Swiss were delaying even though Berne has said it has no objections to the nominations of Wiesel, former Israeli minister Joseph Burg and Avraham Hirshson, head of the Israeli parliament's restitution committee.
"I'm very pleased that they see there is no problem, but then I question why they have not made an announcement yet," Steinberg told Reuters.
"To coin a phrase, if there's no problem, then what's the problem?," he added.

The Swiss government agreed in February to set up the Holocaust fund with 265 million Swiss francs ($181 million) in donations from banks and businesses and said Jewish groups would play a major role by providing three of seven board members.

The cabinet last week named its four members for the fund executive, including Swiss Jewish community leader Rolf Bloch, who is to act as operating chairman alongside Wiesel as representative international chairman.

But Berne drew angry words from the WJC by not appointing the three personalities proposed by the World Jewish Restitution Organisation (WJRO), an umbrella group of Jewish organisations including the WJC and the state of Israel.
The cabinet said it welcomed Wiesel and his two fellow nominees but was waiting for a formal submission by the WJC.
WJC leaders responded that they had long since presented the Swiss side with the three names.
A Swiss government spokeswoman said the cabinet had not acted at its latest meeting on Wednesday because it was waiting to wrap up talks on details of the fund's operation.

"There is no problem with the names proposed by the Jewish side. It is a matter of finishing talks on the modalities of the executive," said Marie-Marceline Kurmann, spokeswoman for the Foreign Ministry's task force on Holocaust issues.
But Stern said all essential details had been settled in talks with Swiss negotiators in Berne last week and confirmed in a letter from himself to Swiss President Arnold Koller.
"I was given the impression that there would be no problem, that all the formalities were done," Stern said.
"I submitted the names in writing, including Elie Wiesel as international chairman, and all the positions as they had been discussed and rediscussed," he said.

Berne's agreement in February to create the fund helped to defuse the country's worst foreign policy crisis since World War Two, sparked by allegations that Swiss banks hoarded unclaimed wealth of Holocaust victims and that neutral Switzerland cynically profited from the war.

The fund is separate from a proposed seven billion Swiss franc Solidarity Foundation that would sell official gold reserves to finance aid to victims of poverty, catastrophes and human rights outrages, including the Holocaust. ($ = 1.464 Swiss Francs)
